speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, February 25, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre):
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are some who have suggested that, given the lack of any really significant initiatives in the Budget introduced recently by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), it was introduced simply because a promise was made that a Budget would be provided during each February; because it had to be done it was done and therefore it did not contain very much.
There are also those who say that in terms of the usual pattern of election Budgets this one was a missed opportunity for the Government. It was in fact a missed opportunity. It was a missed opportunity to be fair. It was a missed opportunity to provide for the future. It was a missed opportunity to be fair because, as all Canadians know, we have a tax system that still lacks fairness. We have a tax system that still has large elements of regressiveness in it. We have a tax system in which the rich seem bound not to have to pay as much as the very poor. We have a tax system in which many corporations go from year to year without paying any tax.
We find that this year, one more time, that the loss in tariffs as a result of a free trade agreement will amount to some $300 million. We have as a consequence, one might infer, the introduction of a tax on gasoline of an additional 1 cent per litre that will cost the average family around $300 additional per year. Once again, it is the little guy who will pay the biggest share of a new tax for a purpose that the average elector has not had an opportunity to approve.
I would note that down our way Canadians often go to Detroit to buy gasoline. When one takes into account the level of taxation on both sides of the border it is true that the tax rate on Canadian gasoline is much higher than it is in the
United States, even though we ought to have an advantage in that area of cost of energy. It is also true that, even if one takes into account the differences in taxation, the price of gasoline is still higher in Canada as compared to the United States.
If one considers the much vaunted tax reform that the Government has introduced, one finds that in spite of all, the average Canadian family of four is still paying $1,000 more than such a family did before the Government came to power. Of course, apart from the element of fairness there is the element of dishonesty. We know that the Government has sales tax changes in mind which will increase the regressive elements in the system. What is more, the lower income and the middle income family will be hurt again.
Of course, you know, Mr. Speaker, that with respect to the element of fairness we have pointed out that there are a number of corporations, some 60,000 indeed, which have managed not to pay any tax at all. The Government has rejected our proposition that there should be a minimum tax on corporations. This is not a radical proposition. It is a proposition which was accepted by the socialist Reagan Government of the United States. It is something that certainly could be emulated here.
When we talk about unfairness, missed opportunity, and the lack of regard for the future, we have to take a look at what the Government has done in the area of regional development. It is true that the Government has articulated a notion that there ought to be a measure of independence and regional control over economic development as in the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, in the Western Diversification Fund, and the initiatives in northern Ontario. When we take a close look at those initiatives, the element of local control is lacking.
More important, if one takes a look at what has been done in Atlantic Canada since the Government came to power, and one takes into account the increases provided in this Budget, it is only going to have returned to it 20 per cent of the funds that the federal Government was previously providing to Atlantic Canada in the way of regional transfers.
There are other elements in terms of future economic development that ought to be attended to. Two years ago the Federation of Municipalities of Canada proposed that some additional $12 billion be provided for the reconstruction of municipal infrastructure. This is a fundamental necessity throughout the country if we are to have the type of economic growth in the future that will provide the jobs that will make it possible for Canadians to prosper, and for us to perpetuate the

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. McCurdy
system of social support and essentially civilized behaviour with respect to the treatment of our people that has grown to be a tradition in Canada.
When one looks at what the Government has been saying about its success in providing jobs, I think that most Canadians will realize that that success has left us all with but certain portions of Ontario without there being an equal and fair share in what job creation there has been.
Even when one talks about Ontario, and hears the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and various members of his Cabinet brag about how well things have gone in Ontario, usually they are referring to the golden horseshoe. When we talk about the need for reconstruction of municipal infrastucture and the need for such things as roads, sanitary sewers, and living up to our obligations on our international agreements with the United States with respect to cleaning up the Great Lakes, and one looks at the unemployment rate in Windsor which is at 14 per cent, we can see that even in Ontario there are areas where Government failures are quite evident.
When talking about missed opportunities with respect to the future, I would like to pay closer attention than perhaps others have done to some aspects of what I think are fundamental failures of the Government. I am fortunate to have youth, post-secondary education, and science and technology as my critic areas for the New Democratic Party.
It is interesting to note all the hoop-la propagated by the Government a couple of years ago during International Youth Year. The Government made huge undertakings to ensure that there would be increased opportunities, and increased opportunities for participation of youth. As Members know, we had a little game of musical chairs that occurred with respect to the youth Ministers, until we reached the point where we now have a youth Minister who pays little attention and says relatively little about youth. Meanwhile, those programs that are supposed to be directed toward youth seem to have lost their priority for the Government.
For example, in regard to the support for student employment under the Challenge programs, in actual funds and in real money allocated for the Challenge program, there has been a continuing drop since the Government came into power. In 1986 S210 million was provided for the summer Challenge program. It has now sunk to $180 million. Of course, with inflation there has been dramatically decreased funds for that purpose.
When one also considers the student loan programs for university students, one finds that we are in a situation where the funds available to be borrowed are inadequate. More important, the emphasis on loans has led to a situation where almost every university student finds himself or herself in the serious difficulty of a huge debt load. By the time of graduation, more than 50 per cent have to carry a debt load of some $10,000.
Yet apart from the organization of study committees, we did not see in the Budget any serious indication that the Government is prepared to engage in serious negotiation with the provinces to come up with a new commitment to support postsecondary education accessibility for our young people. We know that one of the most important elements of real economic growth, one of the real elements in future economic development and prosperity for this country is to ensure that there will be opportunity for all youth.
For the purpose of example, I focus on university and college students. But one can look at the whole scope of action by the Government in respect to increasing opportunity for our young people, and this means not only opportunity for young people but having within our population the capacity for highly qualified work and creativity to contribute to prosperity for the country. The Government has consistently seemed to be unable to address this issue with anything like the priority that it requires.
Let us look at the institutions that our young people are entering with the hope that they may become qualified for future jobs. Through the words of the Prime Minister, the Government promised to improve such opportunity. Through the words of the Prime Minister the Government promised to ensure that the universities and colleges would produce the skilled workforce that we require. If one looks at the pattern one finds that the Government has not only failed to bring about progress, there has been a positive deterioration in the state of affairs. In fact, that has been the case not only since the Government took office, but for the last 10 years.
One thing is sure, when one compares Canada to the other nations against which we must compete, there is among them a higher percentage of participation in post-secondary education, in training, and in apprenticeship than is the case in Canada. Yet we know that the Government has taken away some $2 billion from universities and colleges in the form of transfer payments to the provinces. Over the last decade there has been an increase of 24 per cent in enrollment in universities and colleges, but there has been an 18 per cent decrease in the level of funds.
Our universities and colleges are in a state of deterioration. This fact has been documented in a variety of ways, ways that indicate that the situation is one in which accessibility has been decreased, either by increases in tuition fees, by setting new admission standards which are more exclusive, in the form of libraries lacking adequate numbers of books, in laboratories that do not have adequate equipment, in the form of university professors and college teachers with overburdening loads, or in the form of some of our best scientists leaving because they cannot function in a situation where those institutions in which they work are not being adequately provided for. We missed an opportunity to be fair, not only to those who want to have a university or college education, but to contribute to the future economic growth of our country.
February 26, 1988

With respect to post-secondary education we know that post-secondary institutions have a role in addition to merely teaching. They have a role in research and development. To the credit of the Government, in a variety of ways it has articulated the necessity for real investment in research and development. We can recall that the Prime Minister has pointed out, as so many have pointed out, that unless Canada contributes a good deal more of its Gross National Product to research and development, we must fail in the competition with other industrialized countries of the world. We will fail to mobilize adequately the resources and opportunities which our country presents to us for achieving greatness, as we can.
The Prime Minister promised that we would increase the rate of investment in research and development from 1.3 per cent to 2.5 per cent. Something must have happened somewhere along the line in the attempt to become major league. If one looks at the over-all record of the Government since it has come into power, one sees that the real expenditures on research and development by the Government have actually decreased because of failures in a number of areas.
Just in January the Prime Minister promised that $1.3 billion in new money would be provided for research and development, with the intimation that that would go toward the improvement of basic research in our universities, by providing more money for centres of excellence and for a national scholarship program. The curious thing is that of that $1.3 billion, only about $300 million has been accounted for.
Meanwhile, the Prime Minister's own National Advisory Board on Science and Technology, in the form of the Lortie report, said that basic research was in such a sorry state that we needed to have an immediate investment of a half billion dollars over two years to increase the fundings of granting councils in universities. There was nothing about that in the Budget, not a word.
Here was an advisory council of prestigious membership, with great promise, indicating the focus for the Government, yet a simple recommendation of an assurance of an additional half billion dollars over two years for granting councils, and a subsequent 1.5 per cent rate of increase over GNP growth in those grants, was completely ignored in the Budget.
If one considers Canada's record in research and development, we are tenth among OECD countries and the seventh among the Group of Seven. We need strong initiatives with respect to not only industrial research but to basic research, and both however have been failing.
The Minister responsible for industrial technology has indicated that research initiatives must be subject to market forces. It is true that industrial research should so respond, but I would say parenthetically that even with regard to industrial research the Government has failed. With respect to R and D tax credits we have all kinds of complaints coming from industry about the failure of the Government to provide a
The Budget-Mr. McCurdy
means by which those credits could be returned promptly. As a consequence, many small industries, quite willing to go into research and development, are finding their cash flows affected because the Government has taken as long as two years to process them.
The Government has failed with respect to creating opportunities for youth. It has failed with respect to funding of universities. It has failed with respect to an adequate approach to research and development policy apart from high rhetoric.
In other words, if one looks at such initiatives as the space agency, which is embroiled in all kinds of confusion right now because the Government cannot make decisions with respect to its location, and even though it may be true that the Government has increased the amount of funding for the space program, one sees that it has not adequately dealt with the significant impact of the cost overruns already projected for the space program on our over-all space initiative. The Government is gaining in the race in space, but it is falling far behind in its pace on the ground.
Let me just pause for 30 seconds to say the following about the Government's research and development policy. We are hooked into major initiatives on the part of Europe and the U.S.A. There is no doubt that there can be a significant technological pay-off by involving ourselves in the space enterprise, but recently we have been presented with a real opportunity for a major mission in science that would put Canada number one and would enable us to gain technological pay-offs like nothing else imaginable.
Why does the Government not lead the nation in the direction of our own national mission which would be unique around the world, and consider our capabilities and potential for building leadership in science and technology through the exploitation of hydrogen technology?
I am sorry that I cannot continue to speak about this matter, but I would ask the Government to examine more seriously a new mission, a unique mission, a mission different from that of any other country in the world which would provide for Canadian prosperity and development in the future.
Mir. Redway: Mr. Speaker, I have never heard so much bull in all my life.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Is that parliamentary language?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I think his comments could be characterized, I might say, as full of bull. I could spend 20 minutes dealing with each and every point the Hon. Member has raised, but unfortunately Your Honour will not give me that amount of time, so I would just like to comment on a number of them.
The first thing I can recall is that the Hon. Member referred to a great number of corporations that were not paying any taxes. In fact, as the Hon. Member knows, of the 60,000 corporations which he and his Party talk about as not paying any taxes, about 3,500 of them are large corporations. Of those 3,500, most if not all of them are not paying taxes because of

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. McCurdy
losses in previous years and, under the tax laws, they have the right to recoup those losses before they start paying taxes. Many of those corporations are in the Hon. Member's riding. The balance of those corporations are small and medium sized ones.
Is the Hon. Member really saying that he wants small and medium sized corporations to be wiped out, to go into bankruptcy, to lay off all their workers, just so the Hon. Member can say that everybody is paying taxes whether or not they have the money to do it?
Second, he talked about the Federation of Canadian Municipalities. He said that a couple of years ago it presented a plan for the federal Government to pay a lot of money to help the Federation in paying for infrastructure in those cities. 1 have corresponded and have had discussions with the Federation in that regard, and it had to admit that the economic study it did at that time did not stand up to analysis. The Federation promised that it was doing another economic study with which it would come back to me to justify its claims. That was two or so years ago, and I have not heard from the Federation of Canadian Municipalities since. It has not produced that report or economic analysis to justify the claims it was making.
I see that you are giving me the "hup to", Mr. Speaker. I could go on and on forever. The Hon. Member said that the Government should be fair. I just say to him: "Be fair yourself in the comments you are making".

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to find my colleague becoming so agitated as to use language coming very close to unparliamentary. What he just said would grow a considerable crop itself.
With respect to the Federation of Canadian Municipalities and the precision of its estimates of the needs of municipalities, that may, indeed, be open to question. I will not challenge the Hon. Member's proposition that there was some inaccuracy in its projection. But there can be no denying the needs of the cities of this country. I did not hear the Hon. Member deny that the municipalities of Canada are faced with considerable tax difficulties in getting the resources to do the jobs they are expected to do. I did not hear him deny that the burden has been made more difficult by the policies of the Government in ensuring that municipalities have the funds available to them and on the basis of federal initiatives that would allow them to do the jobs they are expected to do.
More seriously, I did not hear the Hon. Member suggest that some poor devil who was unemployed, who might have been unemployed for four or five years, should have been forgiven his taxes for the next five years. I did not hear the Member address the most significant elements of what I had to say in this Chamber. The Government has not come to grips with the future. The Government has failed to have a research and development policy that will have the impact it ought to
have on science and technology, with the creation of jobs all over the nation.
Nor did I hear the Hon. Member object to my assertion that the Government has failed to provide adequate funds to the regions so the regions could have the opportunity to undertake initiatives to create jobs so they would have as fair a part of the economy of Canada as Ontario has had.
The Hon. Member had all kinds of objections to what I said, but he did not object to the very fundamental of what 1 had to say, namely, that the Government has failed in this Budget to meets its responsibilities for taking initiatives to gain more prosperity for the nation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will remember that approximately two years ago the Government cut the Katimavik program for Canadians, a program aimed at providing a national service for youth in Canada, also providing an opportunity for those young people who had a hard time adjusting to the labour market who needed some new type of supervised experience to adjust to the labour market. The Government has not replaced Katimavik with anything, although the Government said it would have some new kind of program of that nature.
The Hon. Member is the youth critic for his Party. Could he tell us if he has observed whether there is still a need in this country for some kind of national service program for youth and/or a program to help youth with difficulties adjusting to the labour market? From my observation such a program is still necessary. The Hon. Member comes from a different part of the country and dealing with a different group of people. I would like to know about his experience and the need for such a program which was cut by the Government two years ago.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting that in the course of my speech I came to realize that there were so many things which the Government has failed to do I found myself having to talk extremely fast to get in all its failures in 20 minutes. I did not have an opportunity, it is true, to mention Katimavik, but Katimavik is only part of the problem.
As I alluded to, a couple of years ago during the International Youth Year the Government promised that it would develop a policy for youth. The New Democratic Party proposed a coherent policy for youth. The Senate made suggestions about an over-all policy for youth and the Government promised that it would develop a policy for youth. Indeed, the Prime Minister stood in the House and said in March 1986 that we would have a program for youth. It was postponed to May. It was postponed to September. It was postponed to October. The Government appointed a new Minister of State for Youth, and the Minister of State for Youth (Mr. Charest) got lost somewhere along the line. He told me only recently that we will have a program for youth but it will not be until the election and it will be in the form of another promise.
February 26, 1988

We have proposed a coherent program that would provide youths all across this country with opportunities of the sort that Katimavik provided, that would provide opportunities for apprenticeship for training, for opportunities to go to colleges or universities as a person chooses and be supported in the form of an allowance to do so. I have heard rumours that the Minister of State for Youth thought that would be an attractive proposition. Somewhere along the line, I guess being diverted in a premature election campaign tour, he forgot about that. As a consequence, with the abolition of Katimavik and in spite of the promises of the Government, there has been no youth policy proposed or advocated by the Government since the International Youth Year. That is a great tragedy, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, would the Hon. Member elaborate on some of the comments he made about science and technology and, in particular, the space program? He and 1 were both founding members of the Standing Committee on Research, Science and Technology. I have considerable respect for his genuine commitment to improving things in this area.
I want to ask the Hon. Member about the space agency which, as he knows, is a matter of interest to me as a Member from the National Capital Region. Would he agree that Montreal is not alone in having an important aspect of the space industry in Canada and that the space industry is truly a national one with facilities here in Ottawa, Toronto, other places in southern Ontario, Vancouver, Saskatoon and right across the country? It would be regrettable to locate the headquarters of the space agency in any one of the regions; the neutral territory here in the National Capital would be the obvious place to locate it. I say that not just for those reasons-no favouritism to any particular regions-but because we have here, and have had since the 1950s, the administrative and technical apparatus in the National Research Council in the Department of Communications and in other federal Departments and agencies.
In commenting on that, would the Hon. Member comment on the position of the Leader of his Party which, as I understand it, at least as announced in the Montreal area, is that the head office of the space agency should be in Montreal.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think Ottawa has managed to take care of itself reasonably well. One of the difficulties is that the debate on the issue of the location of the space agency has diverted us from the real essential of the problem, and that is to get the operation in train. If something is contemplated, the Hon. Member is in a good position to do it. He is, after all, on the Government side and ought to be able effectively to make representations to the Cabinet to make whatever decision it is going to make immediately. As the Government fiddles, the scientists involved in the space program are burning with frustration.
I have worked with my colleague on the science research and development committee. He is a Member of Parliament I respect and whom I know is very much concerned about
The Budget-Mr. Boudria
science policy. Has he not given any thought to the relative merit of the space program in its entirety as an appropriate initiative with the emphasis the Government is giving it as compared to the alternatives?
The space research program inevitably ties Canada into initiatives established in the United States or Europe as kind of appendages. Would it not be better if Canada pursued the possibility of being able to establish its own unique mission, one for which it has comparative advantage in terms of its resources and opportunities? Why not advocate that the mission for Canada be perhaps in some other area such as the hydrogen technology area?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about Yellowknife?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in this debate this morning. As you may recall, I had an opportunity to speak on the subamendment a few days ago, and I am sure Members across the way will remember it well. But now that we are speaking about the Budget I thought I would just refresh the memories of some Conservative Members about the failures of the Government. I know the Hon. Member for Windsor- Walkerville (Mr. McCurdy) tried to point out a number of those failures. I congratulate him on his valiant effort. However, he had only 20 minutes and it was indeed an enormous task to accomplish in such a short period of time.
During the 1984 election the Tories made promises to many people, as I think I have pointed out in this House once or twice before. One of the promises they made is in the document known as the "PC Pocket Politics". It was that a PC Government is committed to doubling our R and D efforts to 2.5 per cent of GNP in the first four years in office. Since they have been in power they have cut everywhere in the field of research and development. Scientists in the national capital area living in the constituency of the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) sitting across the way, know that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) failed on that promise. They know how badly the Prime Minister failed to deliver. The people of Ottawa-Carleton will no doubt agree with me that the Prime Minister has failed to live up to the promises he made to Canadians.
I want to talk to you a bit about tax increases. You will remember that those Tories across the way made promises in that area as well. You will have a particular appreciation for that because of the fact that you are a non-partisan person and you can appreciate those kind of things in a far more objective way than the Tories sitting across the way, Mr. Speaker.
The Minister of Finance, when he was in opposition, said in a City TV interview on August 28, 1984-very important date because it is my wedding anniversary-that they had no

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Boudria
intention of raising income taxes for Canadians. He said that what we have do is to get down government spending and so on. He said he did not want to increase taxes, that we have a good deal of scope on the expenditure side to deal with the deficit problem. A tax increase, certainly a general tax increase, puts a dampening effect on the economy and he did not want to see us do that.
It was the Minister of Finance who said that. What has he done? Let me tell you the sad reality of the tax increases by the Government. A single earner family of four making $32,000 a year has had a total tax increase since those Tories have been in power of some $1,200 a year. Would you believe it? This from a Minister who promised he would not increase taxes.
If it were an even distribution of increased taxes it would still be a breach of a solemn commitment, a sacred trust, as the Prime Minister referred to it in the past, but at least there would be some equity because everyone would be paying their fair share. Not so. Since 1984 taxes for average Canadians have increased some 68 per cent, while corporate taxes increased by 28 per cent. The friends of the Conservatives, the big business people, have not. had major tax increases, but average Canadians like your constituents and mine have.
Those are not the only promises broken by the Conservative Government. Let me enumerate another and you will no doubt remember it. You probably recall that the Conservatives had a meeting in Halifax, Nova Scotia-you may have read about it in the paper-on August 2, 1984. They called it the Atlantic caucus meeting. Of course, most of the people at the meeting were not caucus Members at all, but that did not matter. At the meeting the Prime Minister proclaimed that he would examine gasoline, alcohol, food and lodging taxes which are reducing the competitiveness of Canada's tourism industry. In other words, clearly indicating to Canadians that what he wanted was lower gasoline prices.

What happened to make the Prime Minister change his mind? Since the Conservatives came to power, the excise tax on gas has increased by 23 cents a gallon. Twenty-three cents! Isn't that outrageous? Mr. Speaker, it's almost enough to make the Hon. Member for Argenteuil-Papineau (Mrs. Bourgault) want to resign. I am sure she must have trouble justifying this kind of behaviour on the part of the Government, considering the solemn commitments made by the Leader of the Conservative Party. Mr. Speaker, this is one more promise, one more solemn commitment that was broken by the Prime Minister. And there are more.

I invite the Member across the way to pay attention. We will ask him questions later.
The Government said with respect to agriculture that it would allow the Farm Credit Corporation to offer agri-bonds so that farmers would have access to reasonably priced funds.
That was the promise. You would think that at least that promise would have been kept. No, once again the spending estimates of the Government came out on February 23, only a few days ago, and do you know how much money the federal Government has placed in the Estimates for the FCC this year? Zero, a grand total of nothing. Nothing for the farmers from the Government. This is not the first time that the farming community is disappointed with the Tories. It is almost a tradition, a tradition that is soon to end, of course, after the next election.
The economic and regional development envelope of the Government in its budgetary estimates has gone down from $14.8 billion to $13.3. What does that do for agricultural development?

And I want to ask the Hon. Member opposite what the cutbacks in the regional economic development envelope are supposed to do for agricultural development?

However, it is nice to know that the Government had money for other causes. Yes, we know that the office of Dalton Camp, which cost zero two years ago, cost $230,000 last year and is budgeted at $261,000 in this year's Estimates. The job of Mr. Camp is to keep the Government out of trouble. He was hired specifically to do that. You can tell what a great job he has done. He has certainly kept the Government in trouble. Just imagine what it would have been like had he not been there? It would have been a disaster. Of course, it is already a disaster.
I could go on with highlighting some of the horror stories of contradictions between the Government's promises and the record. For instance, let me remind you of a promise that the Right Hon. Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) made on September 26, 1984. That was only a few days after he was sworn into office-still a little green. He told the UN that his Government would fulfil a previous Liberal target of directing .7 per cent of Canada's GNP by 1990 to official development assistance. Obviously that is not going to be met. Again, the Government breached a promise. As a matter of fact, the Conservative Government has now pushed that target back by five years according to the November 8, 1984, economic statement.
It has not gotten any better since then. In May of 1985 the Conservative Government cut back further on development assistance. It says it remains committed to the target of .6 per cent of GNP by 1990. Remember that the previous Government had committed .7 per cent. Official development assistance was reduced by $50 million in the following year.
The Budget speech of February 26, 1986, said:
-growth in Canada's aid program will be reduced by $1.5 billion over the
next five years. For the balance of this decade foreign aid will remain at 0.5
per cent of GNP.
February 26, 1988

You can see that the Government is not only weaseling out of previously made commitments but is reducing and changing a solemn promise made to the people of Canada.
The people of my constituency are beginning to be quite upset with the Tories. It is small wonder that the Tories cannot find a candidate to run there.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: They want me.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I just heard good news, Mr. Speaker. They want the Member for Ottawa Carleton to run in Glengarry- Prescott-Russell for the Conservatives. That would be great. The last Conservative candidate in my constituency had the honour of being defeated by the Liberal with the largest majority in Canada. I invite the Member to try to match the record of his predecessor in the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell.
Let me remind you of more broken promises, Mr. Speaker, just to further convince the Government that it is going in the wrong direction, which should be obvious already if it listens to what Canadians are saying. Shipbuilding is a very interesting area and I invite the NDP to pay attention to this as well because we know that their policy is a little confused on that issue. A communique issued at the August 2, 1984, Atlantic caucus said:
A top priority of a PC government will be to create a more viable and prosperous shipbuilding industry. In achieving this goal, we will consult with provincial governments, maritime industries and labour. We will submit the following proposals to these groups during the consultative process.
A second component of their program was "extension of support for Atlantic ship repair facilities and dockyards". We have now seen that the second stage of our frigate program has been delayed. Part of the program has been abandoned. The Government has done everything but deliver on its promises. On February 16, 1986, the Minister of Finance said in this House in his Budget speech:
We are eliminating programs such as... the Shipbuilding Industry Assistance Program.
That was said by the same guy who said he wanted to assist shipbuilding. Under that program which was instituted by the previous Liberal Government and terminated by the Tories shipyards could get a 9 per cent subsidy. Many shipbuilding facilities and organizations including the Canadian Shipbuilding and Ship Repairing Association asked for an extension of that program. However, notwithstanding the solemn promises that the Conservatives made to the shipbuilding industry and the people of Canada, they completely ignored those very important suggestions from the shipbuilding industry and again breached a solemn promise they had made.

Mr. Speaker, I said recently in the House that the Economic Development Committee of the United Counties of Prescott- Russell, and I am referring to the Committee on Industry, Tourism, Agriculture and Commerce, issued a press release. In fact, the Committee chairman, Mr. Denis Pommainville, an
The Budget-Mr. Boudria
elected official in my riding and the Reeve of Cambridge Township, issued a communique condemning the Budget brought down on February 10 by the Conservative Government.
I am glad to hear the Hon. Member opposite say this man must be a Liberal! Shame, accusing an elected official in such a partisan manner. But I am glad to hear it, and 1 want this to be read into the official record of Hansard. I will let Mr. Pommainville know about it, and I am sure the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton (Mr. Turner) can subtract one more vote from the few he might have had if he had run in the riding of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell. His colleague just lost him another vote.
The press release starts with the Committee chairman regretting that the initial economic impact of the Trade Agreement, the so-called Free Trade Agreement with the United States, was mainly negative on rural regions like the one he represents.
In fact the one cent per litre increase in the tax on gas is a tremendous setback for sparsely populated regions, especially those without public transit. Once again, the 12.5 per cent who are unemployed in the area-more than twice the average rate for Ontario-will be handicapped in seeking retraining and opportunities to go back to work, now that owning a car is becoming increasingly expensive.
Mr. Speaker, as you see, this is one elected representative in my riding at the municipal and regional level who is thoroughly disappointed in the Budget brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) here in the House a few days ago.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take the few minutes I have left, and unfortunately they are very few, to talk about the tax on long distance calls. This tax is an affront to people who live in rural areas. Canadians living in these areas often have to call long distance to call the doctor, stores, and even people who live only a few streets or concessions away. This measure is unfair to these communities because although the basic charge is not expensive, long distance calls are. I think putting a 10 per cent tax on freedom of speech is unfair to all Canadians, but it is particularly unfair to Canadians in rural communities and to people who own businesses.

All in all, Mr. Speaker, this is a bad Budget. There was not much to the Budget, it was not a very big document, however, it is not good for the constituency which I represent. I invite the government Members to think about whether or not this Budget is good for their riding. They should conclude, as have I, that it is bad, and they should assist us in defeating the Budget and, while we are at it, in defeating the Government too.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It being eleven o'clock, pursuant to Standing Order 19(4) the House will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 21.

February 26, 1988

subsubtopic: CRITICISM OF MINISTER'S LETTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians find the recent actions of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) threatening to boycott the activities of three Canadian Sikh organizations highly questionable. By conducting a letter-writing campaign against these organizations, some of which were sent to certain Premiers and not others, and some to some federal politicians and not others, it seems that the Minister is reticent in disclosing all he knows to all elected representatives. He should justify the reasons for his recommendations and clarify the allegations against the Canadian citizens within these three organizations by tabling all pertinent correspondence in the House.
It is truly unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that the Secretary of State for External Affairs has tarnished the reputation of Canadians of Sikh origin. The Minister has painted the community with one brush and has opted for collective guilt, instead of pursuing matters of individual responsibility in a sensitive and judicious manner.
Canadian history is littered with examples of communities and collectivities suffering for individual causes. One would have thought, Mr. Speaker, that we would have learned from past injustices.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to call the attention of the House to the fact that the Conservative Government has broken its promises to Winnipeg with respect to maintaining Winnipeg as a transportation centre in western Canada. As was revealed yesterday, it is allowing CNR to downsize the prairie region in Winnipeg to an extent where it will soon become a farce to talk about CN maintaining its prairie region in Winnipeg.
Rather than railroaders, a bunch of maniacal downsizing accountants are running the railway. We will soon pay through the nose for the cost in morale, safety, and other problems that will accumulate as a result of the very bad management decisions that are being made. Tory Members of Parliament from Manitoba have once again failed to protect the interests of Winnipeg. They turned a blind eye, and are sleeping at the switch while allowing the CNR to gut its prairie region headquarters in Winnipeg.

subtopic: SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT LIVES
SUPREME COURT DECISION-CALL FOR LEGISLATION TO PROTECT LIVES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the recent Supreme Court ruling overturning Section 251 of the Criminal Code has left millions of Canadians saddened and confused.
The Supreme Court was not elected to govern Canada. Its role is simply to interpret the legislation enacted by this Parliament.
I, as have all Members of the House, have been contacted by thousands of constituents regarding the Supreme Court decision. These constituents are telling me one thing. They are asking-in fact pleading-that our Government take speedy action to enact new legislation.
Much time has been wasted in the House dealing with the Opposition's wild goose chases trying to slander other Members of the House. This waste of time is shameful when Canadians know that the issue of abortion is critical and crucial to the future of our nation.
On behalf of my constituents, I urge the Government to enact legislation quickly that will protect the lives of all Canadians, both those born and those yet to be born.

subtopic: RETENTION OF PREMATURELY BORN BABIES IN HOSPITALS- LOSS OF MATERNITY BENEFITS
RETENTION OF PREMATURELY BORN BABIES IN HOSPITALS- LOSS OF MATERNITY BENEFITS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a recent CBC TV story outlined the plight of a Vancouver couple whose child was born prematurely and remained in hospital for several months, but because of the limitations of the unemployment insurance regulations the mother was not allowed to postpone taking her maternity leave until the infant was released from hospital and went home, a time when the mother really needed the leave to care for her child.
This is not an isolated case. I have had similar cases brought to my attention and have urged the Minister to make the necessary changes in the unemployment insurance regulations.
Advances in technology and health care mean that many premature infants, who years ago would not have survived, are now able to do so with dedicated assistance from hospital personnel during their first critical weeks. Even after they go home to their parents' care, there are often special medical needs which make it more critical to have a parent with the infant on a continuous basis.
I ask the Minister, knowing his compassionate and caring nature, to move on this matter so that families facing these traumatic situations will have the security of knowing that
February 26, 1988

maternity benefits are available at the time they are most [English]
urgently needed.	POLITICAL PARTIES

maintopic: CONFLICT OF INTEREST ACT-POSITION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES   LABOUR RELATIONS LE DROIT NEWSPAPER-REQUEST THAT PARTIES RETURN TO NEGOTIATING TABLE
CONFLICT OF INTEREST ACT-POSITION OF OPPOSITION PARTIES   LABOUR RELATIONS LE DROIT NEWSPAPER-REQUEST THAT PARTIES RETURN TO NEGOTIATING TABLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since February 20, Francophones in the National Capital Region have been deprived of an essential information tool in their own language.
I am referring to the strike which is dragging on at the newspaper Le Droit, involving some 200 shop workers and newspapermen and affecting over 45 000 readers.
Le Droit has always been a privileged advocate of Franco-Ontarians and this role must continue. A French language daily is a privileged source of information we cannot afford to lose.
This is why I am requesting all Hon. Members in this House to join me in asking both parties to go back to the bargaining table and to find a satisfactory solution to this unfortunate dispute which has already lasted too long.
I ask both Parties, not only in my name, but in the name of my colleagues, to go back to the bargaining table and to come up with a good solution.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT NEGOTIATE AGREEMENT WITH LANGUAGE TEACHERS
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT NEGOTIATE AGREEMENT WITH LANGUAGE TEACHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the position of the Government regarding its language teachers is totally out of line with its support in principle for bilingualism, as expressed in Bill C-72, now undergoing second reading in the House of Commons. Last December, some 800 language teachers strongly rejected the proposed collective agreement which would have increased their teaching workload from 20 hours per week to a maximum of 37 and a half hours, without any preparation time.
If we want that public service employees, some of which are performing very complex and specialized tasks, be bilingual, we have to provide them with apt and professional language training. I therefore urge the Government to put an end to these lockouts and to its refusal to negotiate, and to go back to the negotiating table with a view to achieve a just and acceptable collective agreement, which would allow the language teachers to work as professionals rather than slaves.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT NEGOTIATE AGREEMENT WITH LANGUAGE TEACHERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been reported that the reception by the opposition Parties of the conflict of interest Bill has been lukewarm.
This is not surprising. If the truth were to be known, they are probably shaking in their boots.
Just how ordinary are the ordinary Canadians in the New Democratic Party? Is it only the Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent) who travels around in a chauffeur-driven limousine?
Who pays for the Liberal Leader's (Mr. Turner) $3,000 a month Toronto apartment? What is the connection between Liberal Members and the generic drug firms? Was their opposition to Bill C-22 purely altruistic?
Yes, Mr. Speaker, conflict of interest applies to both sides of the House. No wonder they are lukewarm, or maybe even chilled to the spine.

Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago a team of United States doctors stated in a story in the Ottawa Citizen that Israeli soldiers were systematically beating Palestinians in an epidemic of violence.
Dr. Geiger of the Boston based Physicians for Human Rights stated that they collected medical evidence of violence by the Israeli army on a scale and severity that, if this were a war, much of what they had seen would be regarded as atrocities.
Dr. Jennifer Leaning of Harvard said the doctors observed a systematic pattern of breaking limbs by beatings that is designed to fall short of killing victims.
Sadly, we too witnessed that kind of torture, of beatings, of gross violation of human rights this morning on Canada AM, captured on film, soldiers with rocks breaking the limbs of bound Palestinian refugees.
Again, I ask, I plead, for the Government to show the same leadership against human rights violations in Palestine as it has shown and demonstrated in South Africa.

February 26, 1988

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY IN MONTREAL-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT MAKE ANNOUNCEMENT
ESTABLISHMENT OF AGENCY IN MONTREAL-REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT MAKE ANNOUNCEMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I was recently telling this House that the best speech is a short speech. Therefore, I am asking again: When will this government be courageous enough to declare that Montreal is "spatial"? We have been waiting for months for the government to make that very important statement. Hundreds of thousands of dollars have been spent to make the government aware of how important it is to declare that Montreal is "spatial" and we are still awaiting that decision. What must be done, 1 ask you, Mr. Speaker, for the government to make up its mind at last to declare that Montreal is "spatial"?

Mr. Speaker, the people of northeast Manitoba are in need of an electrical line power. The federal Government can help them to obtain this power.
While the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) has agreed in principle to study this matter, it is essential that a further commitment be made. It is important that the Government undertake to sign a memorandum of understanding committing itself to the development of this hydro line, and to do so in a manner that would involve meaningful native participation.
A hydro line is essential to the livelihoods of over 8,000 native people in my riding. The people of Oxford House, God's Narrows, God's River, Wasagamack, St. Theresa Point, Garden Hill and Red Sucker Lake have all done without a service that most Canadians take for granted. Their struggle to get adequate electrical services has gone on for decades.
Without this electrical line the quality of life in these communities is seriously damaged, and significant industrial development of any kind is next to impossible. We have the opportunity to make a truly significant contribution to the livelihoods of the people of this region. It is up to the federal Government to meet that opportunity.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip's assistant; Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 24, I mentioned in this House that political organizers of the socialist party used and encouraged others to use, in a manner that is illegal and detrimental to Canadian taxpayers, the telephone code number given to the leader of the socialist party, the Hon. Member for Oshawa (Mr. Broadbent).
Mr. Speaker, that use of taxpayers' money to the socialist party's benefit seems to be institutionalized. Last February 22, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) used his mailing privileges to send to people in his riding, following very precise mailing lists, a document entitled The New Democrats, Report from Ottawa. Mr. Speaker, as a representative of a steel-producing centre I would like to comment on the recent ruling in favour of the Canadian steel industry by the International Trade Commission in Washington. I hope that this ruling will help ease the concerns of the American steel caucus with respect to the bilateral free trade agreement. Our steel companies have stayed within the quotas imposed by the Americans, except when the U.S. has experienced a shortage and has turned to Canada for help.
This latest anti-dumping ruling in favour of Canada proves that our steel industry trades fairly. The Canadian Steel Producers Association has been very supportive of the free trade agreement.
With favourable rulings such as this, along with the efforts of the Canadian steel caucus, I have no doubt we will strengthen our current trade relationship under the Government's bilateral free trade agreement.
February 26, 1988

subtopic: DANGER OF DISAPPEARANCE OF LE DROIT NEWSPAPER-CONSEQUENCES
DANGER OF DISAPPEARANCE OF LE DROIT NEWSPAPER-CONSEQUENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in June 1912, the Department of Education in Ontario introduced the infamous Regulation 17 prohibiting for all practical purposes French education in Ontario. Faced with such francophobia, French-speaking Ontarians took a number of steps to claim their right to French education. They founded the newspaper Le Droit which championed the cause of francophones. Over the years, the newspaper has grown to become one of the great dailies of this country. Unfortunately, the very existence of the newspaper is now threatened.
I call upon Mr. Gilbert Lacasse, the employees' union and especially Mr. Conrad Black, to find a reasonable and fair settlement to the labour conflict threatening our daily in the national capital. French-speaking Ontarians want to keep a true francophone newspaper in Ottawa and not an extension of a newspaper coming from elsewhere. The motto of Le Droit, that is "The future belongs to those who fight" is still valid.
We must fight together to preserve the only French daily in Ontario and as soon as the conflict is resolved, I will encourage francophones not only in Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, but on both sides of the Ottawa river, to subscribe to Le Droit and to ensure not only the survival of that newspaper but also its development.

subtopic: COMMITTEE'S IMPENDING VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
COMMITTEE'S IMPENDING VISIT TO BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, next Tuesday the Standing Committee on Justice and Solicitor General, which I have the honour to chair, will begin three days of public hearings and prison visits in British Columbia. These hearings are part of a major review of sentencing, conditional release, and related aspects of the correctional system which the committee has been engaged in since the fall.
In addition to our twice weekly meetings here in Ottawa the Justice Committee will be visiting all regions of Canada between now and the summer recess. After British Columbia we will spend a week in Toronto during the week of March 20.
1 urge all Canadians who are interested in improving the justice system to take an interest in the vital work of our committee.

maintopic: CHINESE HEAT TAX-POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
CHINESE HEAT TAX-POSITION OF PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, prior to the last election, on August 16, 1984, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada sent a letter to the Chinese Canadian National Council which reads as follows:
The Progressive Conservative Party supports the introduction of an all-party Parliamentary resolution which would recognize the injustice and discrimination of the Head Tax and the Chinese Immigration (Exclusion) Act. The Progressive Conservative government would look forward to having discussions with representatives of the Chinese Canadian Community regarding appropriate remedial action and the specific matter of financial compensation.

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-CONSTITUTIONAL POSITION OF PROVINCES
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-CONSTITUTIONAL POSITION OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to address my question to the Deputy, acting, stand-in, substitute, Minister for Trade, whomever that may be this morning. The question I wish to pose to whomever wishes to answer it is an important one.
This morning we have heard reports that the Premier of Manitoba and the Premier of Ontario are now threatening to take the federal Government to court to defend the right of their provinces to implement laws in their own jurisdictions on matters regarding trade. At the same time we know that the U.S. administration and Congress are demanding compensation unless there is full compliance by the provinces. The Government of Canada has caught itself in the proverbial spot between a rock and a hard place.
I wish to ask this question of the Government. Is it not absolutely incumbent upon the Government of Canada to sit down and meet with the provincial Governments to discuss the constitutional federal-provincial problems that have been created by the proposed Canada-U.S. trade deal, and to resolve those problems before any implementing legislation is brought into the House?

subtopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-CONSTITUTIONAL POSITION OF PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister for International Trade will be in the House later. I would like to inform the Hon. Member in the meantime that no Government has discussed any one issue with the provinces more than this Government has discussed

February 26, 1988
Oral Questions
with the heads of provincial Governments the means to implement a free trade agreement with the United States.
As the House will know, the Prime Minister has attended meeting after meeting, hour after hour, to discuss the terms of the negotiation. We have an understanding, an opinion, that there is within the constitutional status of the federal Government the power to enact the legislation that we will be bringing before the House.
I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that the discussions that the Prime Minister has initiated with the provinces in this field will be ongoing.

Mr. Speaker, I see that the Minister for International Trade is now entering the House. I will address my supplementary question to her.
It may be true that there have been prior discussions but the problem has not been resolved. We now have provincial Governments going to court and the Parliament of Canada being expected to deal with legislation that, clearly, could be ultra vires the Constitution of Canada, which could be a major disruption in federal-provincial relations. I ask this question now of the Minister for International Trade.
Would it not be prudent and proper for the Government of Canada to sit down with its provincial counterparts to resolve this major disruption, this major confrontation that is brewing, because of the trade agreement, to determine if there is a way of resolving it? If there is not, they should then go back and reject the trade agreement because it runs counter to the Constitution of Canada.

subtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT POSTPONE INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO RATIFY AGREEMENT
REQUEST THAT GOVERNMENT POSTPONE INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO RATIFY AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is the following. The Minister for International Trade is undoubtedly aware that
there was a Privy Council ruling in the 1930s, the International Labour Organization case, which clearly stated while the federal Government may sign a treaty the provinces may not implement that treaty if it falls within their jurisdiction. There is clearly a point of dispute.
The Parliament of Canada is going to be asked to pass legislation that runs counter to the Constitution of Canada. I would suggest that it would be important for the Government either to resolve that dispute or to take a reference to the Supreme Court before it brings in any implementing legislation.
Will the Government delay bringing in any form of implementing legislation on trade until this major problem with the provinces is resolved, or is the Government once again giving in to the American threat of demanding compensation or concessions? Is that the real motivation for pushing ahead, even though significant provinces in this country are opposed to that particular move because it will take away their rightful powers?

subsubtopic: NEWSPAPER REPORTS OF CONTAMINATED MEAT IN KITCHENER-WATERLOO AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. I wonder if the Minister can confirm reports in the Kitchener-Waterloo Record in the last couple of days which indicate that his Department has received some 220 reports of contaminated meat from some 13 plants in the Kitchener, Waterloo, Guelph area between the period January, 1986, to October 31, 1987. Those reports indicated that meat was contaminated with manure, rust, dust, feathers, hair, and even paint. Many of the meat carcasses were described as slimy, having odours, and discolouration.
Can the Minister confirm that his Department has received reports like that for that period of time, and that even though
February 26, 1988

they were inter-plant shipments the meat could have been shipped across the country, delivered directly to stores, or even sold internationally?

subsubtopic: NEWSPAPER REPORTS OF CONTAMINATED MEAT IN KITCHENER-WATERLOO AREA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have not had the opportunity to read the article. I was informed of the article and, immediately upon being informed of its contents, I requested the appropriate officials in my Department to investigate the situation.
I am sure that all Members of the House, and particularly the Hon. Member who posed the question, would recognize and probably substantiate the fact-and I would be very surprised if he did not-that Canada's meat and food inspection is among the finest in the world. It is supported by the Ontario Veterinary Association, it is supported by the Canadian Veterinary Association, and it is supported by the World Health Organization.
The Hon. Member should be very careful of the manner in which he puts that question, and the manner in which he puts that information. What one has to recognize here is the fact that it is as a result of the best food inspection system in the world that we pick out some of those problem areas and problem products in order that they do not get into the final link of the food chain.

Mr. Speaker, this information is in the public record. Canadians want to know what action the Minister is taking to ensure the safety and health of Canadian food. Surely the Minister does not have to wait until a report appears in the Kitchener- Waterloo Record. Those documents are available to him. We are talking about a miniscule portion of the production and inspection of our whole meat inspection system. If we are looking at 220 reports over a 20 month period then the system looks very lax. The Minister should be taking the responsibility, and not waiting until there is a press report like this, to ensure the safety and health of Canadians and their meat supply.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member should understand that this good work by the meat and food inspectors goes on day in and day out. We do not need a report from the Kitchener-Waterloo Record, nor do we need an article from any other newspaper in the country, nor do we need a question from the Hon. Member in the House. The Hon. Member knows that this goes on on a day-today basis, and that is why we have been able to maintain the best food inspection system in the world.
The other aspect that the Hon. Member should be aware of is the fact that we were requested for information of this kind. I am not sure if it was from the writer of the article to which the Hon. Member refers, but I recall that quite some number of months ago, perhaps even some years ago, or perhaps even before we were in office, a request was made. I do not know whether my predecessor granted approval for the release of
Oral Questions
that information, but I know that I did. The fact of the matter is that we were prevented from doing so because of a court injunction sought by a sector within the industry.
Therefore, it is unfair of the Hon. Member to ask me to make that information public. I am quite prepared to make that information public. However, I cannot ignore, and the Hon. Member cannot ignore, a ruling of a court of Canada. As far as I am concerned, that information should be made available to the public, but we cannot do so.

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PROPOSE AMENDMENTS TO BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall address my question to the Minister and not to the Prime Minister.
The Government makes a few good suggestions in its Bill on conflicts of interest. Unfortunately, with regard to the people's right to a detailed account of the assets of a Minister or Member of Parliament, the Bill states that the Commission can decide to keep such information secret. As this is unacceptable and as there are provincial Governments in Canada and Governments in Great Britain and the United States with systems which are automatically open to the public, will the Government accept amendments to establish a similar system at the federal level in Canada?

subsubtopic: OPPORTUNITY TO PROPOSE AMENDMENTS TO BILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Hon. Member knows, the Government has just tabled the legislation with regard to conflict of interest. The Hon. Member will also know that this is the first time that a Government of Canada has decided to move by way of legislation in this very difficult and sensitive field.
In the legislation we have indicated that there will be an independent commission established to which cabinet Ministers, Parliamentary Secretaries, Members of Parliament, and Senators will disclose their liabilities and assets. That independent commission will have the right to decide what information will be made public.
We believe that an independent commission is in fact the best way to proceed. That does not indicate that as this legislation is debated, and as it comes before committee, changes cannot be made. That happens with legislation at all times.
I would like to indicate to the Hon. Member that this legislation is a big step forward. We think that an independent commission is the proper way to go. There will be no question as to whether or not it will have the right and the jurisdiction to decide what should be made public.

February 26, 1988
Oral Questions

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I compliment the Government on accepting the idea of a commission. I also compliment the Government on the idea that those rules should be applicable to Members on both sides of the House. It is desirable that there should not be an option whether such information is kept secret. All of that information should automatically be open to the public.

OPPORTUNITY TO INTRODUCE BILL ON FINANCING OF POLITICAL PARTIES-GOVERNMENT POSITION

REQUEST THAT NEW LEGISLATION BE INTRODUCED PRIOR TO GENERAL ELECTION

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF ALBERTAN FRANCOPHONES-OPPORTUNITY FOR REFERRAL TO SUPREME COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Supreme Court ruled yesterday that Saskatchewan will have to translate and pass in their French version all statutes adopted since its creation in 1905, or, as an alternative, to adopt a bilingual statute which would proclaim Saskatchewan an English-speaking unilingual province.
This ruling could apply equally to Alberta since this province was also carved out of the Northwest Territories and created by an act which contains the same provisions as the one for Saskatchewan.
My question to the Minister of Justice or to the Acting Minister is this: Is the Government willing to request by referral to the Supreme Court that it confirms that Franco-Albertans have the same linguistic rights as francophones in Saskatchewan?

subsubtopic: RIGHTS OF ALBERTAN FRANCOPHONES-OPPORTUNITY FOR REFERRAL TO SUPREME COURT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Transport said yesterday, the federal Government is willing to provide assistance to the Saskatchewan Government to comply with the ruling of the Supreme Court.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the policy of the federal Government is to promote the equality of both official languages. The Government and myself are willing to consider every option.

On the question with regard to Alberta, I would say at the moment that that question is premature to the federal Government.
