The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilson (Etobicoke Centre):
That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to have this opportunity to rise and add my comments to those of my colleagues on the matter of the Budget that never was brought down by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
The Conservative Government, in its four Budgets so far, has steadily undermined the tradition of budgeting and the tradition of budget speeches being presented before Parliament. We have seen an Olympian Budget-very appropriate because the Olympics are currently underway in Calgary and in his speech the Minister of Finance made reference to them. However, this Budget is not Olympian in its majesty, it is simply Olympian in its detachment from the everyday reality facing Canadians.
The Finance Minister had a real opportunity to move toward greater regional fairness, to redress some of the inequities in the country, to halt rising interest rates which have been rising in real terms, and to make the system fairer. Instead, the Finance Minister basically stood up before Canadians and said "We are saving our announcements for the politically opportune time". He stated that the Government had a commitment to an orderly Budget process but undermined it by introducing only minor changes in this Budget and by failing to address the major problems which are facing Canada today.
On a quick conspectus of this do-nothing Budget we find that in general terms it takes more from consumers, leaves more with corporations, does little for those who are less well off, and does something for those who are well off. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) warned last year that "We are in the process of building two Canadas, one which is rich and promising and one which is under-developed and underemployed". That warning seems to have been lost on the Minister of Finance. I think we should repeat that warning to the Minister of Finance and to the Prime Minister, because if two such Canadas are being built they indeed are the prime architects, willing or unwilling, of the inequities which are increasingly developing in Canada today.
That is something which could easily have been seen by reference to experience of other industrial countries, something which could easily have been provided for in the Government's budgeting process. As I am sure the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance are well aware, if that is allowed to continue it will threaten the very identity of the Canada we have today.
Canada, after all, was founded on notions of regional equity. They are enshrined in the legislative process and the budgetary process. We have such things as regional equalization, regional allowances for higher rates of unemployment. We have not seen that with which a New Democratic Party government would provide the country, a proactive approach to regional development, based not only on the understanding that it is good for areas that are under-developed to be economically developed but also on comprehension of the fact that in the long run the areas in which the economy is overheating are not going to see benefit to their average residents at all, but mainly benefit to those who control the levers of power and wealth in
February 26, 1988

those major cities such as Toronto, in particular, which are benefiting from the economic upturn.
This Budget adds $575 million to the $22 billion total increase in sales taxes since the Government was elected. The cumulative increase in sales taxes is taking $700 to $750 a year out of the pockets of the average family. That makes any cut in income taxes simply an exercise in robbing Peter to pay Paul, taking out of one taxpayer's pocket and putting back into another. Of course, we know that when the Tories do that which is put back is always significantly less than what has been taken out.
The lip service that has been paid to child tax benefits is another defect in the Government's Budget. Instead of concentrating on the sin taxes, the Government seems to have judged that gasoline is a commodity which should be priced increasingly higher, beyond the reach of ordinary Canadians. We have seen the tax on car gasoline. We know it is going to cost more. We know that when the Minister of the Environment (Mr. MacMillan) was the Minister of Tourism he spoke out against higher taxes on gasoline.
Let us not ignore the effect on the aviation industry of the one cent a litre increase in tax. This will drive up costs, particularly for those small operators for whom fuel is a large component of their cost structure. This will marginalize some airlines which have been making it and will jeopardize some airlines which are presently marginal in their operations, particularly the smaller ones.
In my riding of Kenora-Rainy River there are some airlines which operate only one or two planes, strictly for local needs, in air taxi or charter operations, or serving the tourism industry by flying hunters and fishermen in and out of the lake areas. These operations are marginalized by that sort of tax.
The $750 which is taken out of the pockets of average families is reflected by the 21.6 per cent which sales tax revenues are projected to increase this year That is a pretty massive increase in revenues that the Government is predicting. Indeed, it is clearly an indication that the Government's commitment to tax reform is running out of steam. The Government's commitment to revenue generation proceeds full speed ahead, and the Government is losing its commitment to switch from the regressive, inequitable sales tax, which falls more heavily on those with lower incomes than those on higher incomes, to giving the revenue side of the ledger priority.
Average Canadian families want the Government to be called back to its commitment to a more equitable tax system. What they are afraid of, and what the New Democratic Party warns against, is that the Government may be saving such an announcement for sales tax reform until shortly before the next election. The saving of announcements for when they are politically appropriate and politically advantageous calls into question the proud statements of the Minister of Finance that the Government would stay the course with its Budgets and would budget in a business-like fashion. It is clear that the
The Budget-Mr. Parry
Budget is being presented in as political a fashion as even a Liberal Budget ever was.
During the period of the Government's mandate personal incomes have barely kept pace with inflation, but personal taxes will rise more than 16 per cent in 1988. Despite all the lip service that has been given to tax reform, and despite the statement of the Prime Minister that the rich must be made to pay and to pay handsomely, the Government is allowing
60,000	profitable corporations to continue to pay no corporate income tax. That situation flies in the face of equity and also in the face of logic. The Government has stated its need for revenue sources. The Government has given its commitment to deficit reduction. It has not, however, followed the logical next step and gone to the pools of finance which are available to assist in those objectives.
Let me make a simple comparison between the federal Government and the Province of Ontario. In the Province of Ontario every corporation pays what is called a capital tax. This is a minimum tax on corporations. It is hardly onerous. For a small corporation it represents a minimum of $50 a year. That charge goes, obviously, to replenish the coffers of the Province of Ontario. The larger corporations are taxed on an ad valorem basis, a percentage. I believe it is one-fifth of one per cent of their available capital. Every corporation that has an establishment or is registered in the Province of Ontario is paying at least a nominal amount by way of a minimum corporate tax.
Another example is the United States where the Government is at least as conservative as this Progressive Conservative Government-a delightful juxtaposition-as it describes itself. The American Government has seen the real need for a corporate minimum tax and has introduced as part of its tax reform package a 20 per cent minimum tax on corporations.
We are not necessarily talking about onerous taxes on corporations which, for one reason or another, have not reported a profit. We are not even talking of going to the corporations and trying to collect at least some percentage of the money they owe as deferred income taxes which shows up on their balance sheets. We are talking about imposing some nominal degree of taxation at least on corporations which have been very profitable and yet have paid no taxes.
I am sure others have put on the record the cases of individual corporations, including one with profits totalling $117 million and no taxes, another with profits of $220 million and a tax credit of $32 million, and another with profits totalling $39 million and no taxes paid. I am sure other Members have read the names of some of these corporations, so I will not repeat them here.
However, this shows the contrast between those 60,000 profitable corporations that continue to be off the tax rolls, untouched by the Government's revenue garnering measures, and the approximately one million working poor who have

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Parry
been added to the tax rolls as a result of the federal tax reduction and only partial indexation of the tax system.
1 am sure other Government Members will rise with pride to say that the Government having more people to the tax rolls is good because it indicates that more people are working and therefore paying taxes. However, they will be either ignoring or wilfully concealing the reality that while many taxpayers have come on to the tax rolls as a result of an increase in their income, many are earning no more than they were earning four years ago in terms of real dollars but are paying taxes now when once they were not.
The Government pays lip service commitment to child care in Canada through this Budget. Child benefits have been cut because of deindexation in past budgets and there is no substantial improvement to that in this Budget. From 1989 onwards the child tax credit will be limited to an indexation factor of the amount over 3 per cent, which guarantees a 3 per cent decline in real terms of the dollar value.
The cumulative effect of deindexation of child benefits is that by 1991 the child benefit system will be reduced by about $1.5 billion, approximately one-third. Obviously, that is significantly larger, in fact a multiple of the amount that the Government envisages putting into a child care program. Again, this is evidence of the Tory syndrome of saving three times as much on the swings as it is prepared to spend on the roundabouts, even after it has advertised such a strong commitment to child care in Canada, after it had trumpeted its initiatives as providing solutions. Of course, those measures merely paper over the cracks of the existing problem.
One of the most significant measures the Government could have taken in the Budget to increase prosperity, promote economic growth within Canada, and to try to work toward a better life for Canadians, was to reduce the interest rates that Canadians pay. Many economists believe that the so-called trade agreement between Canada and the United States, even in its most favourable manifestations, does not have even one-half the economic potential that a drop in interest rates would have in promoting Canadian business.
Presently, Canadian interest rates are kept artificially higher than those in the United States in order to shore up the value of the Canadian dollar, but also to assist the Bank of Canada in its futile attempt to bring inflation down to a zero percent level. Reducing inflation to zero per cent is a prime example of erecting a macro economic measure into an instrument of policy. Of course, the inflation rate is nothing more than a macro economic measure.
Fortunately, Canadians have economic choices which they continually use in making decisions about the mix of goods and services that go to support and essentially make up the lifestyle that we enjoy. Each and every one of us, in our qualities as spenders, are continually involved in controlling inflation by deciding on what and what not to buy. Canadians may choose not to buy strawberries when the price is too high, or switch vegetable and meat choices as the price fluctuates. Inflation is
a macro economic measure that is very useful but, as a target, zero per cent inflation, which has overtaken the minds of the Bank of Canada and been erected into a priority, is essentially a proxy goal of very limited utility.
None of us want to go back to the days of the Liberal Government when inflation was allowed to run riot and interest rates soared to levels of 21 per cent to 23 per cent for ordinary mortgages. Everyone wants to control inflation, but we as parliamentarians must demand of the Government that it pursue a reasonable policy that trades off inflation control for economic development, instead of completely neglecting that economic development for the goal of controlling inflation.
Economists have estimated that an 84-cent dollar is the point at which we become non-competitive with the United States, so that attempting to keep the dollar value below the 79-cent or 80-cent level provides a very substantial margin in which Canadian business and Canadian industry is still competitive.
The Premier of Quebec is the fondest friend of the Prime Minister on many issues. While the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) may deplore that fact, he is powerless to change that by any jot or tittle. However, the Premier of the Province of Quebec said on February 8 that there should be lower interest rates and that any further increase will jeopardize our exports.
The fact is that if interest rates in Canada could be reduced by approximately 1 per cent there would be increases in output and employment that would, even in as short a period as five years, exceed even the notational gains that the Government's most favourable studies postulate as a result of the trade deal.
A cut in rates would help the average consumer. Consumer spending accounts for approximately 60 per cent of Gross National Product and if growth is to continue consumer spending will have to remain high. A cut in interest rates would substantially reduce the cost of servicing the Government debt, and that would leave more money for important social programs and job creation.
The Budget itself estimates that a 1 per cent decrease in interest rates will cut the deficit by $1.4 billion in one year and by $9.5 billion over four years. Certainly that would be a measure that this Party could endorse as being very substantially effective, not only in deficit control but ultimately in increasing the revenue side of the ledger, as more people would be working.
The Budget fundamentally ignores the fact that unemployment in eight of the 10 provinces remains at recession levels. There is no commitment to increase the very nominal funding that was granted to northern Ontario by means of the FED-NOR program. There is no commitment to the promotion of industrial development in other parts of the country.
The Government had led Canadians to expect that the Budget process would be done on a businesslike basis. It has
February 26, 1988

led Canadians to believe that Progressive Conservative budgets would always be substantial, would be responsible, would be full of measures that would be significant even though people may not like them. On all three scores, the Government has retreated from that commitment.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that one of the key planks of the Conservative Party when it ran for election was its move to eliminate national debt and to reduce the deficit. In the three years that it has been in power it has managed to increase the national debt by 50 per cent to about $100 billion. It has decreased only marginally the deficit. Will the Hon. Member comment on this inadequacy in the operations of the Government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I suppose we all stand to be judged somewhat harshly for our election commitments. Of course the Government must expect, being in the position it is in, that it will receive the harshest judgment. The fact is that during the election campaign the Conservative Party protested loud and long about the situation of the deficit that previous Liberal Governments had run up by, to use some common phrases, uncontrolled spending, spending like drunken sailors, or having let the economy get out of control. The fact is that for all its vaunted skills and commitment the Government has really made very little impression on the deficit.
Why has it made little impression on the deficit? I suggest it is partly because the commercial interests that brought the Government to power and which back it so powerfully did not feel that it was ultimately in their best interest to see the deficit reduced because, of course, they would have been the ones called upon to contribute to such a reduction. The fact is that the income tax situation which I outlined previously in my speech is obviously to the advantage of the corporate sector. While we hear great preaching from the corporate sector about the need for deficit reduction, as is characteristic in such cases, and individual taxpayers are not any different in this regard, there is very little volunteering done to reduce that sort of deficit.
Other matters I could mention deal with the unwise commitments that the Government has made to military spending, something that will not benefit Canada's defence and which, as we all know, will have a very limited impact on Canada's economy.

speechtext: Resuming debate with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there was a time in the House when speeches on the Budget were an opportunity to examine a blueprint of economic and social priorities for the country. It was an opportunity for Governments to give an honest rendering of the financial accounts of the nation. At such a time they had to be forthcoming about prospects for growth and development. Most important, it was a time when they attempted to set out some series of goals and objectives that the Budget, the most important economic document of the country, would seek to implement.
One of the difficulties of engaging in this debate is that that is not what the Budget brought about. It was a masquerade, a camouflage, a subterfuge. It was cosmetic. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is known as the "Mary Kay" of the political world. All he does is to put a lot of rouge and lipstick on the same old face. He does not provide Canadians with an opportunity to examine clearly the fiscal and economic direction of the country and what the Government will do about it. There was an attempt to present a picture of rosy, glossy, Pollyanna scenarios without providing the facts. When one examines that document it is disturbing to realize how much was hidden. There was a deliberate attempt to hide
within the Budget Papers the real story of economics in this country. Let me provide one example.
For the past two years we have been given the impression that the proposed trade initiative with the Americans was going to be the great cornucopia of economic growth and development. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Minister of Finance promise you everything. You have a bald head, hair will grow; you have warts on your fingers, they will come off; all you have to do is to sign this agreement with the Americans. The Prime Minister goes to Calgary and says, "You see all those people driving BMWs in Toronto? Sign free trade with the Americans, and everybody in the West will have one too". This was going to be the magic wand that would open up all manner of incredible opportunities.
However, one need only look at the Government's own documents, which are not something that the Liberal Research Bureau has concocted. Let us look at the Department of Finance's own document, its own economic forecast as to the prospects under the trade agreement.
I think it is a fair assumption that the Department of Finance is on the same side as the Prime Minister. Perhaps in their hearts they are not, but as public servants they will be required to give the best case scenario. What was stated in the Department of Finance document, the Government's own estimate of what trade with the Americans will provide? Well, Mr. Speaker, hold on to your hat on this one. It stated that maybe, possibly, under the best case scenario, we may get one-half of one per cent growth per year. That is not even within the margin of error of the computer that does the forecasting. It is so small as to be meaningless in terms of an economic forecast.
The Minister of Finance rises in the House to the cheers of all his back-benchers and states that the Government will create 120,000 jobs. He did not say that those jobs would be spread over five years. That is 24,000 jobs a year. Last year, in the month of January, the Canadian economy created 60,000 jobs. We have been doing that for 10 years. In other words, the economic growth prospects provided by the Department itself are marginal. Not only that, but the Department of Finance forecast did not include two very important items, which we found out when we had to go through the Budget Papers. What they did not account for is that the Government of Canada will lose revenue as a result. In four or five years' time when the agreement is finally in place, it will mean $2 billion a year of lost revenue. Even in this year there was a very interesting little table in the fiscal plan which stated that lost revenue due to trade initiative amounted to $450 million, and increased taxation on gas was $475 million.
In other words, every time a Canadian taxpayer fills up his or her car with 30 or 40 litres of gas, he or she will be paying a lot of money for "Brian's folly". The Department of Finance did not include the fact that there was going to be increased taxation on Canadian consumers to pay for the trade initiative. It is $.5 billion this year, $1 billion the next year, and finally
February 26, 1988

$2 billion a year. That wipes out that one-half of one per cent growth per year.
Furthermore, the Government includes absolutely no forecast in its analysis as to the cost of adjustment. It pretends that that will not be a problem. Industry after industry has come forward and stated that there will be major job loss. Someone will have to pay additional UI premiums. Someone will have to pay for additional training. Someone will have to pay for new industries in the community that will be devastated by the loss of its textile plant, food processing plant, or its printing industry. Who will pay for that? The federal Government has stated that it will not pay for it. The provinces or the private sector will pay for it. The Macdonald Royal Commission has stated that that could be a $5 billion tab.
Try these mathematics, Mr. Speaker. The Government states that there will be one-half of one per cent of growth. If one subtracts $2 billion in additional taxes and $5 billion in adjustment costs, not only is the additional growth wiped out but there is a negative account.
Last Monday in Fredericton Mr. Archer McLean appeared before the federal Liberal task force. He is a vice-president of McCain Foods, the largest food processor in Canada. There are 1.7 million Canadians who work in the agro-food business. Mr. McLean appeared before the task force and stated that his company has a choice under the free trade agreement; it either shuts down or goes south. That is his choice. I have it here, and I will gladly table the document. Mr. McLean stated that the agro-food business, the people who put the cornflakes in the box, the tomato catsup, the frozen foods, or the chicken pot-pie, which is a big industry in Canada, cannot survive under this free trade agreement.
If the Government is being honest, they will be required to pay higher input costs for the tomatoes, the potatoes, the chickens, the asparagus, the broccoli, and all the foodstuffs used. As Mr. McLean properly pointed out, the trade agreement forgets a couple of important ingredients. One, Canada has a winter that sometimes lasts six to eight months. Therefore, if a company has to compete on the so-called level playing field with chickens that are grown in Georgia, where a little hut is built and some corn is thrown on the ground, and that is all that has to be provided, compared to chickens that are grown in New Brunswick, Manitoba, or British Columbia where the buildings have to be heated and many other input costs have to be provided, they say that they cannot compete. They say that they have a choice of getting rid of supply management, put import quotas on, which is not free trade, or they will move south.
There is an interesting example in my own province provided by Mr. McLean. There is a large plant in Portage La Prairie where 300 or 400 people work. They make French-fried potatoes from good Manitoba potatoes. They pay $120 per tonne for potatoes in Manitoba. That same tonne of potatoes is available down south for $90 a tonne because of the difference in climate and geography. It has nothing to do with the
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
creative ability of the Canadian farmer, his sense of confidence or entrepreneurship. All it says is that he has to grow potatoes in a cold climate. Therefore, there are higher input costs.
The Government of Canada has taken none of that into account. It is putting at risk the largest industry in Canada. Where is that contained in the Minister of Finance's forecast? Where is his analysis of how we will compensate that industry or the workers who will lose their jobs? It is nowhere to be found. The economic forecast provided by the Minister of Finance in his statement is phoney. It is a con job, it is a snow job, it is has no basis in reality or in fact.
I did not mention the printing industry which will lose
10,000	jobs, or the textile or garment industry which has been promised that it will not be injured by this trade arrangement.
[Translation)
The largest industrial sector in Quebec is the textile and clothing industry. This sector would certainly be substantially weakened by the Free Trade Agreement.

Yet the Government makes no provision. It states that it will not do anything about it. Yet it knows that someone will have to pay the tab.
Let us look at the analysis on the economic side. The Government is hiding the facts. It is concealing the truth. It is relying on its propaganda machine rather than on its ability to present an effective argument. That is not right. Canadians should expect more from the Government. They should expect honesty and truth from their Governments, otherwise how can they prepare themselves and know what they are getting into?
Let me provide another example of the way in which the Budget is cosmetic. The Minister of Finance promised new initiatives in the regions to help them regain their economic balance, one of the primary responsibilities of any Government. He promised the great Western Diversification Fund. However, when we look at the Estimates we find that the money being spent on western diversification is under old programs, that certain provinces do not receive any money at all, and that in my own Province of Manitoba they are hauling out jobs. Some 300 jobs in the CNR will disappear, but the Minister of Transport says "Oh, I am sorry, that is downsizing". So we have this interesting contradiction-we have a Western Diversification Fund with no allocation. They have not got around to it yet because they have not completed the organizational principles. They are taking money under existing regional development programs, transferring it out of my province to go elsewhere, and reducing jobs in federal Crown corporations. That is the Tory formula for regional development. They take away money, take away jobs, and leave us with a lot of propaganda and promises; hardly a basis upon which to build confidence.

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy
Let me give another most fascinating example by returning to the trade agreement for a moment. The Government of Canada says: "We want to be world traders", but we know from an analysis that it is really preoccupied with Canada-U.S. trade. I would be most happy if a Member on the government benches would answer the following question: If the Government is anxious to encourage trade around the world, why is it that it has reduced the budget expenditure on trade development by $11 million in the last year? Why is it cutting back? It has cut back on export financing every year. Is it any wonder that our trade with the Pacific Rim is down by 30 per cent? Is it any wonder that our trade with Europe is down by 20 per cent? Is it any wonder that our trade with the Middle East is down by 30 per cent? It is because this is a Government which does not want to trade with the world. It wants to trade only in Akron, Ohio, or some other such place. It is deliberately neglecting its responsibility to the Canadian business sector to provide the export financing, the development work, and the embassies and consulates necessary to open new trade opportunities. That is the real agenda. It is not interested in trading around the world. It has no interest in supporting such trade diversification for Canadian industry.
Can we believe a Government which is going to spend $11 billion on nuclear submarines but is cutting back millions of dollars on trade development? What kind of a perverted sense of priority is that? What kind of rank stupidity is it when the Government is going to build submarines to satisfy the adolescent aspirations of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Beatty) who was frustrated because he did not have enough submarines in his bath tub as a young boy and as a result cut back expenditures on broadening our trade position around the world?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Shame on you, Lloyd.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no shame about that. The only people who should have shame are those who are engaging in a gross militaristic expenditure at the sacrifice of our trade development in the Pacific Rim, in Latin America, and in Europe, and who are sacrificing small businesses that need export financing support to open up new markets, for the sake of an adolescent fantasy of cold war brinksmanship that the Minister of National Defence tries to peddle around the country.
Let us deal with another question on which the Government has been totally silent. The other day when 1 was in my riding in Winnipeg, I met with a group of social workers and street workers to talk about the problem of the homeless in downtown Winnipeg. We have 5,000 homeless kids in downtown Winnipeg. Many of them are engaged in street prostitution. Many of them are running from home to home. Many of them do not have the kind of support they need. There are 5,000 homeless kids, to say nothing about families.
However, if I turn to the Estimates I find that the Government is cutting back job-creation programs dealing with low income people. It is cutting back its expenditures. Also,
CMHC is no longer providing financing to housing for special needs. Grants are being cut back to the social agencies, and organizations working with native groups. In other words, at a time when we are facing one of the most debilitating and heart-wrenching social problems of a generation, the Government says "no", is indifferent to the problem, and is paying no attention. It cannot be heard.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about International Year of the Homeless?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. We had International Year of the Homeless, as my colleague reminded me. Where are the programs which came out of it? There were conferences, studies, reports, and research, but no direct delivery. Those
5,000	homeless kids-and the numbers are growing-did not see any of that money. In fact, I will give an example. The Government announced a few years back that it would spend $5 million to try to do something about battered and abused women and children as a result of the Badgeley report.
I went through the figures. All the money that has been spent to date went on conferences, seminars, and training programs, with the exception of one project in Vancouver that actually provided direct delivery to the children themselves; one of the whole group.
I only use that example to say that the Government does not have its priorities straight. It has no social programs. It has no sense of what is happening out there on the streets. It is abandoning those people. It is cutting back on its support in critical areas.
There are Members of the House who have stood and defended the so-called Canadian Jobs Strategy program as being a great accomplishment. What that program has done is taken money away from those very groups. They say that they are going to train for the labour market, which means that they are not training those children who left school in grade seven or grade eight and do not have the proper literacy to enter a training program. They do not give money to social organizations such as children's homes or Rossbrook House in downtown Winnipeg which used to use those programs to take native kids off the street and give them some initial experience in the job market. Oh, it was not fancy training on computers, but it sure made a difference. It gave them a step up and a sense of hope. All that has disappeared, and now we are left with a problem which is growing by leaps and bounds, and we have a Budget which says absolutely nothing about it.
What we say is that this is not a Budget. It is an attempt to fool and con the Canadian people. It is a blueprint for discrimination. It is a blueprint of bias. It is a blueprint that has no feeling or compassion.
This is why Canadians, when they begin to learn what is in the Budget and see the reality behind it, will make their judgment, as they are already making it, that this is a Government which no longer has the right to govern.
February 26, 1988

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
1 have a question for my hon. colleague, Mr. Speaker. I listened with interest to a speech on priorities in which the Hon. Member said that priorities seem to be skewed with this Government and the Member laid out a whole number of reasons why he felt that.
I want to ask him about another priority, namely, we appreciate as Members of this House that the mining industry is one of the major industries of Canada. It is a multibillion dollar industry employing tens of thousands of people in every region and every province. One of the initiatives that Governments have taken in the past has been a mechanism called flow-through shares. This mechanism allowed mining companies to raise funds for exploration. If you like, the first stage of any mine development has to be to find the mineral deposit and explore it. We know now that the Government has decided to phase out for all intents and purposes that flow-through program which, in a sense, leaves the mining sector high and dry, particularly the small and medium-sized junior companies which are exclusively Canadian owned.
Could the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) say whether this too would be part of his litany where the Government has missed the point in its priorities by abandoning support for exploration at the front end of the upstream of mining development in Canada? Will that have serious implications on the ability of Canada to develop this critical sector in the future?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis) for his question. When I was in British Columbia seven or eight months ago meeting with the mining associations it was very clear that the flow-through share program was one of the most important regional development programs in the country. It was a program that not only had a specific set approach but also had a number of corollary benefits for the communities and the regions. The Member himself knows from the constituency he represents that many small communities are totally dependent upon the mines. If the exploration and development is cut back, reduced or eliminated, then the communities themselves suffer.
We had commitments from the Government that it would do something for the mining industry. The flow-through share program was removed and the Government said it would replace that with something, but, as we know, the Government takes off one shoe and never lets the other one drop. So we have the abandonment of the flow-through share formula but nothing to replace it. I have had several representations from the mining industry in my own province that this situation is creating a climate of uncertainty which means there will be a cut-back on investment and expenditure. It will also have harmful effects on many of the small one-industry mining towns which are very important in western Canada. Once again we have a Government that has blinded itself to reality as to what works well and what it should be doing to keep a regional balance in Canada.
The Budget-Mr. Axworthy

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to put a genuine question to my friend from Winnipeg-Fort Garry. I have had some concern and, frankly, some surprise in my mind since reading the comments after the policy conference in Vancouver on the question of the trade deal with the United States. I know that in his speech the Member made a very strong condemnation of the potential effects of this trade deal, one that I share completely. I would like a reaffirmation from the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) as to the Liberal commitment on this trade deal.
If a new Government is elected, a non-Conservative Government, a Government which includes or is made up of Liberals, will that Government take a decision to see to it that the trade deal as it stands, as an agreement, is not put into effect but is instead replaced by a series of individual initiatives to improve our trade with the United States, as opposed to this blanket, across-the-board deal and what I think we both feel has been so devastatingly dangerous, a deal for Canada which has led to so many surrenders for this country?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to answer the question. Perhaps the Hon. Member who referred to the policy conference in Vancouver would be interested in a speech given by the Leader of our Party. May I just take a moment to quote from it. He said:
I oppose the Mulroney trade deal because in integrating our economy and
society more closely with that of the United States we are dramatically
reducing our ability to make our own choices for our own future.
I think it states very clearly the position of the Leader of our Party and it is a position supported by the caucus of our Party. We are determined that this is a deal, an arrangement, that is not in the interests of Canada and would have to be abrogated.
I point out to the House, and I do respond to the sincerity of the question with an equally sincere answer, that when we were in Washington a week ago as part of a fact finding mission to determine American attitudes about the deal, it was clear to me that it would be far more difficult to abrogate a treaty after it is ratified at the end of the year than if we were to do it now. The Americans would not find it particularly difficult or problematic if Canada, through its democratic process, decided that it did not want to go ahead with the deal. It would be more complicated if after ratification and the treaty or the agreement was signed and the abrogation had to be used, it could cause a reaction. That is why I think it is absolutely morally responsible for the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) to call an election before that ratification so as to give Canadians the right to decide on this issue, among others, before we put ourselves into the situation where Americans might have more justification for reaction.
I am not saying that we would pull back from that reaction. I am just saying it would be more difficult. If the Conservatives really believe and have the strength of their convictions, which I sometimes wonder if they do, then let them put it to the test and not put a future Government in a position of having to abrogate a treaty. Have an election before the

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Hovdebo
agreement is ratified. If the Conservative Party wins, then fine, the Conservatives will have a clear mandate and they can go ahead and ratify in all good conscience. If they lose, they will not be putting a future Government into a difficult position. That, I think, should be a clear recognition on the part of the Prime Minister. If he had any sense of responsibility or obligation through the democratic process, that is what he would do.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) in the early part of his speech referred to the document prepared by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) concerning job creation if the trade agreement was put into effect. My colleague referred to the tax increases to replace the duty removal that will be the result of this deal.
Could the Member tell me if in this report of the Department of Finance the Department took into consideration the changes in the value of the dollar? Was the assumption that the dollar would remain at 74 or 73 cents? As of this morning it was at 79 cents, and this increased value of the Canadian dollar could wipe out completely the benefit of the duty removal. I would like the Member's comment about this aspect of the Department of Finance's report on job creation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will provide a very quick and concise answer. First, it is very clear, almost axiomatic, that if this agreement goes ahead, there will be an increasingly upward valuation on the Canadian dollar. That is the expectation of the Americans and it has been the case historically when such agreements have been signed. There will be new institutional pressures to bring that about. We can make the assumption that the dollar will be much higher than 79 cents after ratification.
There has been no consideration whatsoever in the Department of Finance report that the value of the dollar is a factor that should be taken into account. If the value of the dollar were to change by another three or four cents, it would totally wipe out any proposed benefits under the forecast provided.
I will just say as a footnote, Mr. Speaker, because I know that you are deeply interested in these matters, that I met yesterday with people in the softwood lumber industry who pointed out that they have already been severely affected by the change in the value of the dollar from 75 cents to 79 cents. They are already losing markets and are already on the margins of production for small and medium-sized sawmills on the West Coast, in Quebec and in Ontario. Already the promises we have had from the Government that somehow the dollar was a fixed item have been proven wrong in a very vital sector of the industry. My colleague is absolutely correct. The Department of Finance took no consideration of that.
The Department did not consider the cost of adjustment nor did it consider the cost of increased taxes or the cost of the dollar. If all that had been taken into consideration in an
honest forecast, we would probably have a negative report, not a positive one.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 appreciate the opportunity to speak on the Budget. When the Minister of Finance made his Budget Speech, he used a format which to some extent has been followed by other Hon. Members who have spoken. When he spoke, he reported on his term of office. On some occasions, it was a somewhat biased report, but it was a report on that period of time. Over the days of the budget debate, government Members who have risen have followed that format. They have repeated ad nauseam the same liturgy, attempting to convince the people of Canada by repetition that the Government has done something worthwhile in the last three or four years.
Since the Minister has established that format, I am sure he will not object to our use of it. I will use at least part of my 20 minutes, therefore, to report on the record of the Government and on the effect of the Minister's Budget on the people of Canada.
This particular Budget contained very little. I suppose that this is part of the reason for the Minister having used the format he did. He really did not feel that he could spend the half hour or so he thought was necessary talking about the new deal he was presenting to Canada. Therefore, he made a rather lengthy attempt to put the past in the best light possible.
The Budget will have very little impact on Canadians across the board. What becomes important in the Budget is what the Government is attempting to make the central issue in this debate. The Budget does nothing to improve Canada for Canadians. The Budget contained a few things that will impact negatively, particularly taxes, and it even contains some retreats from positions the Government had taken previously. However, there is nothing to make the life of Canadians better than it was before 1984 when this Government was elected.
The record of the Minister of Finance in agriculture has not been impressive over the years. He started out early in his career by presenting to Parliament and the people of Canada a paper entitled Finances in Agriculture. I believe it was presented late in 1984 or early in 1985. The main point of that paper was that the farming sector was obviously the richest sector in the economy and that farmers were getting much more out of the economy than they should. That was two years ago, and that was when the recession in agriculture began.
At that time, even the Minister's colleagues in the Conservative Party were embarrassed by the lack of knowledge and understanding expressed by that paper. The Minister withdrew from the ideas in that paper rather hurriedly and buried his head for a while. Rather than getting good advice on agriculture, his next incursion into the agricultural industry was to remove the investment tax credit on new machinery. He, along with his colleague in revenue, began to investigate how producers had benefited from the investment tax credit.
February 26, 1988

We recognize that the agricultural industry is not doing particularly well at this time. The Minister's initiative kind of put the boot to the industry when it was down. At a time when a great many farmers were suffering, they suddenly found themselves being investigated for doing their part in helping the machinery industry.
The investment tax credit for new machinery was put in place to increase the movement of machinery from the manufacturer to the farm by giving some assistance to the farmer. This was of great assistance to the farm-machinery manufacturing industry. The provision was not put in place originally to help the farmer, although farmers did receive some benefit from it. It was intended to increase the sale of farm machinery, and it did just that.
The Government proceeded to remove that measure and to assess farmers who had made use of it. It was a kind of harassment which caused a great deal of concern and heartache among farmers who were already in a bad situation. Again, the Government retreated in somewhat of a fluster. I must say that, for a while at least, the harassment stopped. The Government decided that its approach to this withdrawal was doing it some political harm and it withdrew. Now, however, many farmers are telling me that they are again being assessed and are required to produce rebates on matters into which they themselves had very little input. It is the kind of discrimination that gives all Governments a bad name. After the Government committed itself not to proceed with investigation and harassment of farmers who had taken advantage of the investment tax credit, it is now proceeding to do so. It flip-flopped twice on that issue.
Another incursion into the agricultural industry was the Minister's White Paper on taxation presented last June. In that paper the Minister attempted to impose accrual accounting on all farmers. With a certain amount of relief, farmers are seeing one further retreat by the Minister in this Budget, but he did not solve the problem. He left farmers in limbo. He says he is going to take his accounting and tax procedures to hearings across the country and then come down with something somewhere between cash and accrual accounting. Right now farmers do not really know what to expect. They can carry on what they have been doing for at least another year, but they have not been told whether they will be faced with accrual accounting in the future.
The Minister's inadequacy or absolute lack of knowledge of agriculture almost makes you want to take him out West and say to him: Now, Mr. Minister, this is a cow. This is a quarter section of land, 160 acres. It is part of a section which is a mile each way, one square mile or 640 acres. Those kinds of things are basic to agriculture and the Minister should know them, but he apparently does not because he does not take the kind of action which will allow farmers to continue to operate. It appears that he does not know the effect of the decisions he
The Budget-Mr. Hovdebo
and his Department have made in the past concerning the farm industry.
When you look at the rest of the Budget, you realize the Minister lives in some kind of a fantasyland which must be based on Bay Street. He does not deal with reality. His is a financial world which has very little connection to the actual world of day-to-day labour and production.
For example, the Minister tells us loud and long in his speech about the reduction in income taxes for ordinary Canadians. He says they will receive an average reduction of S400. Yet he neglects or overlooks or fails to tell the people of Canada that since 1984 the Government has added $1,400 to their taxes. The average family is paying $1,400 more in taxes now than it was three years ago. Yet the Minister stresses the fact that you might get $400 back, even though you are out of pocket by $1,000. This is not something for rejoicing, nor is it a particularly realistic or honest approach.
I can give another example. The Minister suggests the Government has created one million jobs. Using the Government's method of counting he says they can prove it. Yet he ignores the fact that about half those jobs are part-time and that in eight of the 10 provinces the unemployment level has not changed significantly.
Another example. Even as the Minister proclaims fairness in taxation for all people, he adds another five cents a gallon to the price of gasoline as of April 1. That makes for a total increase in the cost of gasoline of approximately $350 more than it was in 1983. Since many workers, even those in fairly low-paying jobs, cannot avoid using their cars, this is a regressive tax. The people who can least afford to pay it and who are required to use their cars must pay it. It comes off the top of their earnings before they spend money to live, pay rent and buy food.
A further example. After great huffing and puffing by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) about the increase in research and the need to double spending in that area, we have a recognition of specific funds in the Budget for research. Research happens only if you plan and train for it. The Government has systematically reduced the funds available for higher education. Places like the University of Saskatchewan, in my province, which is one of the most active and highly respected agricultural research centres in Canada, are not being adequately funded to train scientists let alone carry out the research necessary in that area.
I am sure that if you took any particular sector of the economy you would find exactly the same thing. By reducing the number of scientists or the amount of money going to training and research facilities, the Government is effectively reducing the amount of research being done in Canada. We are tenth among the OECD countries in the amount of money we spend on research. We are short of scientists and we are not giving universities enough money to produce scientists. We are

February 26, 1988
The Budget-Mr. Hovdebo
not taking advantage of the opportunities available in technological development. Again, the Minister is living in a fantasy-land or in Bay Street finance land rather than in the world of development.
The Minister spends much time spouting about fairness, but his projected taxation structure is anything but fair. To most of us, fairness in taxation means that those most able to pay should pay a higher percentage than those in the lower income tax brackets. Since 1984 corporation taxes have risen by 28 per cent, yet personal income taxes have risen by 55 per cent. Sales taxes which everyone in Canada pays when buying anything have risen by 96 per cent. There are still 60,000 profitable corporations which pay no taxes at all. The Minister did not even suggest a minimum tax so that all corporations would contribute to running this country.
The Minister has not moved on reduction of the deficit. In the three and a half years during which the Government has been in power it has added $100 billion to the national debt and has only marginally reduced the speed at which the debt increases each year. I can go on. There are 200,000 child care spaces required and no effective money to solve the problem. There is only marginal money available to proceed on regional development.
We are studying the effect of this Budget on Canada. Free trade is not the answer. That is the road to Americanization and America is not the model toward which most of us want to move. Joining the United States is not a new deal for Canadians. During the rest of the Government's term I hope it will bring to the people of Canada a new deal which recognizes that we need improvement and the development of Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have great respect for the Hon. Member who just spoke. I served with him on the Public Accounts Committee and I regard him highly. However, I must say that I found his remarks today to be basically bumf.
He referred to the issue of personal income tax and the amount of income tax paid by individuals as opposed to corporations. The Hon. Member did not point out that while the amount raised by personal income tax has increased very substantially in the last three and a half years, 80 per cent of that increase is as a result of the fact that people have been put back to work. People who were not working are now working and earning money again and are, therefore, paying taxes. The Hon. Member did not point that out in his comments.
The Member also spoke about the deficit and deficit reduction. The Member indicated that there had been only marginal deficit reduction over the last three and a half years. You and I are aware, Mr. Speaker, that the annual deficit has been reduced over that three and one-half short years by $10 billion. The other day an Hon. Member suggested that "billion" should be spelled with a capital B, and that is right. There has been $10 billion annually spent on deficit reduction.
If the Member believes that deficit reduction should take place at a much more substantial rate, would he increase personal income taxes or other taxes, a move which he and his Party have opposed consistently over the last three and a half years and forever before that, or would he cut government expenditures, a move which he and his Party have opposed over the last three and a half years and long before? They have indeed consistently requested that government spending be increased over that period of time. How would the Hon. Member reduce the deficit-by cutting expenditures or by raising taxes?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for the question. He is using exactly the same logic in commenting on my speech as the Government is using across the board. The Member suggests that the deficit has been reduced by $10 billion. That may be so, but in the process of doing so the Government has increased the debt of Canada by $100 billion.
The Government shows the same kind of logic in dealing with employment. One million jobs have been created, but each of the provinces has the same percentage of unemployment as they had before and the number of part-time jobs has increased. Half of the one million jobs were part-time jobs.
The Member asks how we would reduce the deficit. We certainly would not do it by signing a trade agreement with the United States because the effective result of that will be the reduction of jobs. We need to put in place a policy of full employment which will require domestic investment. Every $1 billion of profit in a Canadian corporation produces close to
5,000	jobs. For every $1 billion of foreign profit 16 jobs are created and most of the profit goes to the foreign country.
If we really want to get rid of the deficit we must put everyone to work, whereupon taxation will increase to the extent that the deficit will become less and less of a factor.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to ask a question of the Hon. Member and I am sorry that it may not be as complimentary to the Conservatives as my questions usually are. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) is a very wise Member. Does he know that since the Conservatives came into power in 1984 a family of four with one earner earning $32,000 a year pays $1,200 per year more in income taxes than it did the day prior to the Government coming into office? I would like the Member to tell us what he thinks of that particular government initiative.
I would also like to ask the Member about tax on long distance phone rates, the tax on free speech as I call it. That 10 per cent tax on telephone rates unfairly discriminates against rural Canadians. I know the Member has a number of rural constituents because I had the honour and pleasure of visiting the Hon. Member's riding last year. He was kind enough to greet me when I went there. He and I both represent rural ridings.
February 26, 1988

Would the Member not agree with me that that tax which will generate $870 million this year is totally reprehensible and discriminatory against rural Canadians and small businessmen, the same small businessmen whom the Tories pretend to represent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the first part of the question regarding the income and taxation of the average family is a matter of record. Taxation has increased by $1,300 or $1,400 and the reduction will only be about $400 if it goes through in the way the Minister suggests.
With regard to the 10 per cent tax on telephone calls, there are communities in my constituency where every call made is a long distance call. If people want to call their doctor, their children's school, or call for any equipment or supplies, they have to make a long distance call. Small businesses in such communities are bearing the burden of the major increases in the tax on telephone calls. There is no doubt in my mind or in the mind of anyone in rural areas that the 10 per cent tax on telephone calls is very discriminatory.
It affects people in rural areas much more than it affects any city dweller.
